results.summary: The design is a 16-microphone delay-and-sum beamformer that processes PDM inputs and outputs beamformed audio via I2S. It expects a 3.072 MHz bit clock and 48 kHz LR clock, and can use up to 16 digital microphones. Documentation is minimal placeholder text, so the internal beamforming details and test procedure are not described. The project is notable for targeting a high microphone count in a small digital design.

This project implements a 2x2 matrix multiplier that receives two matrices over UART and transmits the resulting matrix back. It also provides the four result bytes on parallel output pins, and operates with a 100 MHz clock and a 115200 baud UART interface. The design was tested using a USB-UART bridge and documented with example test cases, including notes on overflow for results exceeding 255. The project credits mentorship and was completed as a student project.

This is a 4-bit successive approximation analog-to-digital converter that converts a constant analog input voltage to a 4-bit digital output. It requires an external sample-and-hold circuit to keep the input stable during the 5-clock-cycle conversion, and a 5 MHz clock, producing a 1 MHz conversion rate. The digital result appears on four output pins with an end-of-conversion signal. The design is purely analog and includes no digital interface beyond the ADC outputs.

DaDDS is an 8-bit direct digital synthesizer intended as an RF transmitter with on-off keying and frequency-shift keying modulation. It uses a 60 MHz clock and outputs an 8-bit DAC word, and includes UART control for setting frequency and modulation parameters. The documentation is sparse, consisting mainly of images that are not accessible in the provided text, so the exact control protocol and test method are not fully described. External hardware suggested includes a DAC and RF circuitry in a typical application diagram.

This is an analog design that biases a standard inverter for linear-mode operation, effectively creating a simple amplifier. It has one analog input and one analog output, and requires an external 20 nF capacitor and a small-signal sine wave to test, with an oscilloscope for observation. The documentation is extremely brief, providing only the title and a minimal test suggestion. This appears to be a basic analog building block or educational experiment.

The design is a resubmission of a simple VGA ray casting game engine that renders textured walls in a 3D-like first-person view without a framebuffer. It is controlled via an SPI interface for player point-of-view and other visual effects registers, and outputs standard VGA signals. Optional external QSPI memory can supply textures, and the chip includes debug and demo modes. This is a more complex design occupying 6x2 tiles and represents an iterative development from earlier Tiny Tapeout versions.

This project is a test chip for a 24-bit VGA digital-to-analog converter with a digital control block that generates various test patterns. The analog DAC outputs need external op-amps and a VGA connector to be used. The design includes multiple test modes and a pass-through mode, and the documentation notes potential issues with matching and slew. It is primarily a characterization and prototyping vehicle for analog VGA output.

AtomNPU is a 4-bit neural processing unit designed to perform multiply-accumulate operations for neural network computations. It has 4-bit input and weight inputs and produces a 4-bit output, operating at 100 MHz. The documentation is very thin, with only a one-line description and placeholder text, so the exact MAC architecture and test procedure are not specified. It is a compact implementation of a basic NPU building block.

This design reads a 16-bit design ID from an I2C EEPROM and generates control signals to select the corresponding Tiny Tapeout project on a multiplexer. It also outputs the read value on a UART for debugging and includes a ring oscillator that can be enabled to provide a clock, avoiding the need for an external clock. It requires an external I2C EEPROM and pull-up resistors on the I2C lines. The design is a prototype for automatic project selection in Tiny Tapeout.

The Morse Code Keyer converts dit/dah paddle inputs into Morse code outputs, including auxiliary dit/dah signals, a buzzer tone, and a 7-segment display of the last character. It supports straight key or iambic paddles (types A and B) and adjustable speed from 7 to 110 WPM via dip switches. The design emphasizes proper radio keying practices, warning against using the auxiliary output directly for transmitter control, and recommends a companion PCB for interfacing with radio hardware. It operates at 12 MHz and outputs to a seven-segment display.
